migrationNotes: SPINE: Start by clapping a nursery rhyme and discover that the hands follow stressed syllables. Then trade the rhyme for Shakespeare, learn how the same pulse sits in pairs of syllables, and finish by letting the line stretch, flip and take names, ending where we began with falling feet.

lesson.title: Metre and scansion

lead.text: Clap along to a nursery rhyme and you will find that your hands do not land on every word. They land on some sounds and skip others. To see which, break each word into its syllables, the chunks you say with one push of breath. Hickory has three syllables, hick, o and ry. Dickory has three as well. Dock has one.

Say “hickory dickory dock” aloud and you tap only three times, although you have said seven syllables. Some syllables are louder and longer than the rest. We call those the stressed syllables, and the others are unstressed. The stressed ones are the beats that your hands find.

afterFigure.text: Two counts are now in play, and the rest of the lesson depends on keeping them apart. Syllables are everything you say. Beats are the stressed ones among them. A poet who wants the ear to settle chooses words so that the beats come at regular spacing, and that regular pattern of strong and weak syllables is what we call metre. The next step is to look at the patterns poets use most.

lead.text: Say the first line of the rhyme at an even pace. Your hands will want to tap on the stressed syllables and skip the rest.

Many nursery rhymes start on a beat: HICK-o-ry, HUMP-ty. Much of English poetry does the reverse. It starts with a light syllable that leans into a heavy one, the way you say “hello”, with the weight on the last syllable. A pair of syllables with the weak one first and the strong one second is called an iamb. “To-DAY” and “be-LONG” are each one iamb, with the capitals marking the beat.

An iamb is a foot, which is the name for one repeating unit of a line. Poets name a line by its foot and by how many feet it holds. Five iambs in a row make ten syllables with a beat on every second one. The Greek for five is penta, and a metre is a measure, so this line is iambic pentameter. Shakespeare used it for most of his plays and for his sonnets, and its rhythm sits close to the way people speak English, which is part of why it is easy to listen to.

afterFigure.text: The figure marks the stressed syllables in two such lines. Read each one aloud and lean on the marked syllables. You should find the pattern pulling you along, a light syllable and then a heavy one, five times over.

lead.text: Say the first line of Sonnet 18 slowly, and tap once for each vowel sound. Do not count words; count syllables.

reveal.text: Ten, with the beats on I, pare, to, sum and day. That is five iambs, so the line is iambic pentameter.

lead.text: With the pattern in hand you can mark up any line. The marking is called scansion. You write out the syllables and decide which are strong, then you compare them with the pattern. In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables, the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth. The odd-numbered ones are the weak syllables between them.

Speech and pattern do not always agree. In the first line of Sonnet 18, “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?”, the word “to” is light in everyday speech and you would hurry past it. The pattern puts it in a beat position. The best reading sits between the two. “To” gets a little more weight than usual, and the line moves in time.

To scan a line, count its syllables first. Then mark which ones are strong and compare them with the pattern. The next screen does this for a line by Milton, and the one after asks you to carry on alone.

steps.headline: Scan “They also serve who only stand and waite”.

lead.text: This is the last line of Milton's sonnet on losing his sight. Follow each move in turn.

workedSteps.text: Count the syllables: they, al, so, serve, who, on, ly, stand, and, waite. Ten.
Mark weak and strong in turn, starting weak: they AL so SERVE who ON ly STAND and WAITE.
The five beats sit on every second syllable, so the line is iambic pentameter.

steps.headline: Place the beats of “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”.

lead.text: This is the third line of Sonnet 18. The first two beats are placed for you, and you carry on from there.

workedSteps.text: Count ten syllables: rough, winds, do, shake, the, dar, ling, buds, of, May.
The first beat is on “winds” and the second on “shake”.
Keep going in steps of two syllables.

reveal.text: You stepped through the line two syllables at a time. The rhythm is regular, and the light words sit between the heavy ones.

lead.text: Every line so far has had exactly ten syllables and ended on a beat. Shakespeare's lines sometimes run over. In Macbeth, when he hears that his wife has died, he says “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”, which is eleven syllables. Marked for the beat it reads to-MOR-row AND to-MOR-row AND to-MOR-row, with all five beats on even-numbered syllables and a weak eleventh syllable left over at the end.

afterFigure.text: The extra syllable does not change the metre. The line still has five beats, so it is still iambic pentameter. That is why a line is named by its beats. Count the feet first, then check whether a spare syllable hangs off the end.

lead.text: Sonnet 116 describes love as a fixed mark that looks on storms without being shaken. Line 6 is below. Count carefully, tapping once for each vowel sound.

reveal.text: Eleven: “-ken” trails after the last beat on “sha-”, so the line has a feminine ending and is still pentameter.

steps.headline: Falling feet and the names of lines

lead.text: Every foot so far has risen, weak then strong. Turn it round so that the strong syllable comes first and you get a trochee. Most nursery rhymes are built from trochees because they start on a beat: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR. The last foot has lost its weak syllable, which is common in rhymes. When you clapped along earlier you were counting trochees.

The foot and the number of feet together name a line. Two names to learn: a line of three feet is a trimeter and a line of four is a tetrameter. Five feet give the pentameter you already know. Four iambs make iambic tetrameter, which has eight syllables. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter. Length changes the feel. A longer line has room to think, and shorter ones feel brisk, closer to song.

afterFigure.text: Set the two lines side by side and the difference is clear. One rises towards each beat and the other falls away from it. Two lines can hold similar numbers of beats and still feel quite different, depending on which way their feet face.

lead.text: Use what you know about the names of lines. A foot of this kind has two syllables.

Shakespeare's witches in Macbeth chant to a different beat from his human characters. Say their line aloud, DOU-ble, DOU-ble, TOIL and TROU-ble, and notice which syllable of each foot carries the beat.

reveal.text: The witches chant in trochaic tetrameter. Each foot falls, and the last weak syllable is dropped. Shakespeare gives his supernatural speakers a metre unlike his humans' iambic speech.

lesson.orientation: Count syllables and place the beats of iambic pentameter. Hear a feminine ending, and tell a rising iamb from a falling trochee.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Think of a nursery rhyme you learned before you could read. Without deciding to, you probably said it with a steady pulse, and if you were sitting down your hand may have tapped along. The words did not ask for that. Something in the way they were chosen and ordered made the pulse hard to avoid.

Verse has always worked like this. Before a poem says anything, it sets up a beat, and the ear settles into it the way it settles into the ticking of a clock. Shakespeare's sonnets, Dickinson's hymn-like stanzas and a rhyme for toddlers all lean on the same machinery, a pattern of strong and weak sounds repeated line after line.

This lesson starts with a nursery rhyme and ends with a line of Shakespeare. On the way you learn to count the sounds in a line, find where its beats fall and name the pattern. You need only your ears and a finger to tap with.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count syllables, place the beats of iambic pentameter and tell a rising foot from a falling one.

recap.keyIdea: Metre is a pattern of weak and strong syllables. Iambic pentameter has five rising feet, ten syllables and beats on the even ones.

blocks.text: You tapped the beats of a nursery rhyme, counted ten syllables in Sonnet 18's first line and placed the third beat on syllable six. You found the eleventh syllable in Macbeth and in Sonnet 116, and heard the witches' falling trochees. The rhyme you began with turned out to be built the same way.

recap.nextHook: The beat is one thing a line can do with sound. The next lesson looks at the sounds themselves, and it starts with a tongue-twister that trips your mouth on purpose.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'
hints: Say the line slowly and tap once for each vowel sound.
'Compare' and 'summer's' have two syllables each.
Every other word has one syllable; add them up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ten: shall / I / com / pare / thee / to / a / sum / mer's / day.

questions.onCorrect: Ten: shall, I, com, pare, thee, to, a, sum, mer's, day. Each beat sits on every second syllable.

misconceptions.feedback: “Summer's” has two syllables, not three. Tap once for each vowel sound.
“Compare” and “summer's” have two syllables each, so a syllable is missing from your count.

questions.prompt: In a regular line of iambic pentameter the beats fall on the even-numbered syllables. Counting from the first syllable, on which syllable does the third beat fall?
hints: List the syllable positions that carry beats.
The first beat falls on the second syllable.
Each further beat comes two syllables later.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

questions.onCorrect: Syllable 6: the beats fall on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the beat's number. The question asks which syllable it falls on, counting from the start of the line.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in 'That looks on tempests and is never shaken'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Tempests', 'never' and 'shaken' have two syllables each.
Notice what follows the last beat on 'sha-'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Eleven. '-ken' is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat on 'sha-': a feminine ending.

questions.onCorrect: Eleven: “-ken” is an extra unstressed syllable after the last beat, a feminine ending.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for a regular line. This one has an extra syllable at the end.
“Tempests”, “never” and “shaken” have two syllables each. Recount.

questions.prompt: The witches chant 'Double, double, toil and trouble': DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble. Each foot falls from stressed to unstressed. Name this foot.
hints: Its Greek name means 'running'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb. Four trochees make trochaic tetrameter.

questions.onCorrect: The trochee: stressed then unstressed, the reverse of the iamb.

misconceptions.feedback: An iamb rises, weak then strong. The witches' foot does the opposite.
A dactyl has three syllables. These feet have two.

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in Dickinson's 'That perches in the soul'?
hints: Tap once for each vowel sound.
'Perches' has two syllables.
Count the remaining one-syllable words and add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six: that / per / ches / in / the / soul. Three iambs make iambic trimeter.

questions.onCorrect: Six: that, per, ches, in, the, soul. Three iambs make iambic trimeter.

misconceptions.feedback: “Perches” has two syllables. Tap it twice.
Check that you counted “perches” as two syllables and not three.
That counts feet. The question asks for syllables.

questions.prompt: A line has four iambic feet, as in 'And sings the tune without the words'. Name its metre: iambic what?
hints: The Greek prefix for four comes before '-meter'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Iambic tetrameter: four iambs, eight syllables.

questions.onCorrect: Iambic tetrameter: four iambs make eight syllables.

misconceptions.feedback: Pentameter has five feet. Count the iambs in the line shown.
Trimeter has three feet. Count the iambs in the line shown.

questions.prompt: Clap along to “Twinkle, twinkle, little star”, once on each beat. How many claps do you make?
hints: Say the line aloud and tap along.
Tap harder on the strong syllables.
Count only the strong taps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four: TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR, one on each stressed syllable.

questions.onCorrect: Four. You clapped on the strong syllables only, and that regular pulse is what metre counts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every syllable. You clap only on the strong ones.
There is a clap on each of the four strong syllables. Say it again and tap.
That counts words and syllables together. Clap only where the stress falls.

questions.prompt: “com-PARE” is an iamb. Does its beat fall on the first or the second syllable?
hints: Say “compare” and listen for the louder syllable.
questions.onCorrect: The beat falls on the second syllable. An iamb is a weak syllable followed by a strong one.

misconceptions.feedback: Say the word aloud. The strong syllable is the later one.

acceptedIdeas: It has ten syllables in five weak-strong pairs.

hints: Count the syllables in each line. Which has one too many?

questions.prompt: How many syllables are in a line of iambic tetrameter?
hints: How many feet does tetrameter have?
How many syllables does an iamb have?
Multiply the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four iambs of two syllables each make eight.
